newameRica provides a ggplot2 theme and color palette system built on New America's data visualization brand guidelines. This guide covers the core workflow: session setup, a bar chart, a line chart, and saving your output.

## Prerequisites

Install Chivo from Google Fonts before using the package. Search "Chivo" at fonts.google.com and install via Font Book on macOS, or right-click → "Install for all users" on Windows.

Then install the package:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("newamerica-graphics/newameRica")
```

## Session setup

Load the package and ggplot2 (or tidyverse), then call `na_set_defaults()` once. This sets the global ggplot2 theme and default geom colors for the session.

```{r session}
library(newameRica)
library(ggplot2)  # included in tidyverse — either works

na_set_defaults()
```

If you have Whyte installed and are preparing charts for publication, switch to it now:

```{r whyte, eval = FALSE}
na_register_fonts("whyte")
```

## Bar chart

Use `na_theme_bar()` for vertical and horizontal bar charts. It sets bar-specific grid and axis styling, and automatically adds a zero baseline.

```{r bar}
df_bar <- data.frame(
  category = c("Category A", "Category B", "Category C", "Category D", "Category E"),
  value    = c(42, 67, 31, 55, 78)
)

ggplot(df_bar, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  na_theme_bar() +
  labs(
    title   = "Chart Title",
    subtitle = "Subtitle or supporting description",
    caption  = "Source: Example data"
  )
```

For horizontal bars, swap the `aes()` mapping and pass `horizontal = TRUE`:

```{r bar-horizontal}
ggplot(df_bar, aes(y = category, x = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  na_theme_bar(horizontal = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "Chart Title",
    subtitle = "Subtitle or supporting description",
    caption  = "Source: Example data"
  )
```

## Line chart

For single-series line charts, `na_set_defaults()` handles everything.

```{r line}
df_line <- data.frame(
  year  = 2015:2024,
  value = c(12, 15, 14, 18, 22, 20, 25, 27, 24, 30)
)

ggplot(df_line, aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2024, 2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Chart Title",
    subtitle = "Subtitle or supporting description",
    caption  = "Source: Example data"
  )
```

## Saving

Use `na_save()` instead of `ggsave()` directly. It uses the ragg device for correct font rendering and applies size-appropriate font scaling automatically.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
na_save("output/bar-chart.png", size = "medium")
```

Size presets:

| `size` | Width | Height | Pixels | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `"small"` | 3.25 in | 2.5 in | 975 × 750 px | one column in a two-column PDF or digital layout |
| `"medium"` | 6.5 in | 4.5 in | 1950 × 1350 px | standard digital report charts (default) |
| `"large"` | 9 in | 6.5 in | 2700 × 1950 px | complex or dense charts that may need more space |

To save the last plot at a specific size:

```{r save-explicit, eval = FALSE}
p <- ggplot(df_bar, aes(x = category, y = value)) +
  geom_col() +
  na_theme_bar() +
  labs(title = "Chart Title", caption = "Source: Example data")

na_save("output/bar-chart.png", size = "medium", plot = p)
```
